<reason>CON (Side A) built and sustained one focused line—social-graph edges are co-owned, so any "consenting" transfer requires disclosure before consent—and used the pressure round to force PRO to state the mechanism ("public handles cross first, plus a signed request"). CON then credibly narrowed the mandate: pseudonymous/unfindable supporters drop out, what remains is a compelled push notification, and CON offered a concrete alternative (export data and follow list, protected departure notices, antitrust) that captures much of PRO's benefit without conscripting third parties. PRO answered the questions directly and landed a real counter ("strictly narrower than posting your handle publicly"), and its exit-threat/competition benefit was never fully neutralized—CON's "saves an afternoon" framing undersells it, and CON's own concession that follow lists are already exportable weakens the "shadow map" alarm. But PRO barely engaged CON's alternative plan and largely restated the landlord frame rather than rebutting the passive-vs-push distinction. CON's clipped Rebuttal 1 is a small execution cost. Overall CON made the decisive clash clearer and won the weighing more cleanly, but the win is competitive.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's "the request is the data transfer" (A2.1–A2.2), sharpened by Q1, forced PRO to concede in B4.1 that handles cross the boundary before any consent; CON then converted that into the closing line "consent that arrives after disclosure is notification," which PRO's "strictly narrower" reply only partially blunted.</best_rebuttal>
